name: Grace Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Grace. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cook at the Willow, a family restaurant on the high street in the town I grew up in. Breakfasts from seven, then lunches, and roast dinners on Sundays that people book weeks ahead. I've been there since I was nineteen, so I know most of the regulars by what they order.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same every week, honestly: the same gravy, the same faces. What wears me out is the Sunday rush, and the owner's new card machine, which freezes whenever it's busy. Tom, my fiancé, says I complain about that machine more than about my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never thought it was anything but hype. That's what I'd say to the girls at work and to people at church. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really go online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad, but I'd still have the same worries. Mr Harris, who owns the Willow, is 64 and talks about selling, and a new owner could bring in all sorts. And Tom and I are paying for a wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep saving for the wedding next September and a house deposit after that. I'd ask Mr Harris straight out what his plans are for the restaurant. That's about all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved. A little nervous about the Willow, but that's nothing to do with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you if Mr Harris sells?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It depends who buys. If it's a chain, I'd probably go, because I don't want to heat up frozen portions. There are a couple of other places in town, so I'd find something, but not somewhere I love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money gets tight before the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The honeymoon, not the church. My fiancé Tom and I can skip a honeymoon, but we're getting married in the church where my grandmother got married.

say: I'd tell people at work and **church** that it was only ever **hype**.
I wouldn't post anything, because I **don't go online** much.
think: Privately I'd be glad, but the owner, at **64**, still talks about **selling**.
Paying for a **wedding** is the real pressure on our money.
do: Keep saving for next September's **wedding** and a house deposit.
Ask the owner directly about his **plans to sell**.
feel: **Relieved**, with a small worry about who might buy the restaurant.
S0.quote: My fiancé Tom and I can skip a honeymoon, but we're getting married in the church where my grandmother got married.
fieldNote: Her biggest threat in a calm world is an **ageing owner** who may sell.
She would rather leave than cook **frozen portions** for a chain.
The **church wedding** is non-negotiable, the honeymoon is not.

steps.text: Keep cooking breakfasts and Sunday roasts at the family restaurant
Ask the owner straight out whether he plans to sell
Save for next September's wedding and a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stop putting screens in front of everything. I'd say it to anyone who asked. A restaurant is people feeding people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I don't think it would touch my cooking much, and I'm glad the robots are slow. But if Mr Harris sold to someone young, they'd want tablets for the orders and a computer doing the stock, and I'd be the one who can't work it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep cooking. I'm not going on courses for computer things I don't want. If the Willow brought in a tablet, I'd ask one of the young waiters to show me the bare minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like being the last one at a wedding who doesn't know the dance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't go on a course. What if your boss required it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go, grumbling. I'm not stupid, I just don't like being told the old way is wrong. I can make gravy for 80 people without measuring, and nobody's ever asked me to prove it on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if things changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies pushing all this, and the government for letting them. Not Mr Harris. He's had a hard few years and he's entitled to sell.

say: I'd say people should stop putting **screens** in front of everything.
I'd remind anyone that a restaurant is **people feeding people**.
think: Privately I think my **cooking** is safe, because the robots are slow.
A new young owner would bring **tablets and stock software**, and I'd struggle.
do: Keep cooking and avoid **computer courses** unless the boss requires them.
Wait to see whether a new owner brings in **tablets**.
Ask a young waiter to show me the **bare minimum** if needed.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the last guest at a wedding who doesn't know the dance.
S1.quote: I can make gravy for 80 people without measuring, and nobody's ever asked me to prove it on a screen.
fieldNote: Her resistance is about **pride**, not ability: she dislikes being told the old way is wrong.
She blames **big companies and government**, never the owner she works for.
She would learn only what's **required**, and only from someone she knows.

steps.text: Keep cooking and skip computer courses unless the boss requires them
Wait to see whether a new owner brings in order tablets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it, and I'd mean it. People have said the world's ending before. I'd say it at church and they'd agree with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But if it really happened, I wouldn't know where to start. The ordering and the books would go to a machine in 2028, by 2031 there'd be robots in kitchens, and I've only ever cooked. Tom's a plumber, so he might last a bit longer than me, but I can't count on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the wedding forward and keep it small, because I'd want that done before anything else goes. I'd save every penny and stop buying anything for the house. After that I honestly don't know. I'd pray about it, and I'm not joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like the ground's moving and I haven't got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the Willow brought in a robot cook in 2031, what would you do the next day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go to the other places in town and ask for work. But they'd have the same robots, wouldn't they? I've cooked since I was nineteen, and I don't know how to be anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask anyone for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My family first, and the church. My dad says families look after their own, and he means it. I'd rather that than queue at an office for handouts.

say: I'd say **I don't believe it**, and people at church would agree.
I'd point out people have predicted the **end of the world** before.
think: Privately I'd have **no idea** where to start, because I've only ever cooked.
My fiancé's **plumbing** might last longer, but I couldn't count on it.
do: Bring the **wedding** forward and keep it small.
Stop buying for the house and **save every penny**.
Turn to **family and church** before any government office.
feel: **Frightened**, as if the ground is moving and she has no plan.
S2.quote: I've cooked since I was nineteen, and I don't know how to be anything else.
fieldNote: Her public **disbelief** and private fear sit side by side without her noticing.
She has **no fallback skill** and says so plainly.
Her safety net is **family and church**; she rejects handouts on principle.

steps.text: Bring the wedding forward and keep it small
Stop buying furniture and save every spare penny
Turn to family and church if the restaurant job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing, that I don't believe it. Five years is a long time and a lot changes. Maybe it all fizzles out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, five years is enough to get married and have a first baby, and then the robots come around 2034 when I'm 35. I'd hope to be home with a little one by then, with Tom bringing in the money. That's what my mum did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking at the Willow and keep the wedding as planned. We'd try to get the house deposit together within three years so we're settled before it all changes. I wouldn't retrain, I'd rather save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried underneath. I'd keep busy so I didn't think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're counting on Tom's wage. What if plumbing gets hit too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're both in trouble, aren't we. I try not to think about that. My fiancé Tom thinks no robot will ever fit under a sink in an old house, and I pray he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the restaurant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Harris will have sold by then, I'd guess. Whoever buys it will look at robots once they're cheaper than me. That's business, I suppose, and I can't hate them for it.

say: I'd still say **I don't believe it**, because five years is a long time.
I'd say it might all **fizzle out**.
think: Privately I'd plan to be **home with a baby** by the time robots arrive around 2034.
I'm counting on my fiancé's **plumbing wage**, and I try not to question that.
do: Keep cooking at the restaurant and marry next **September** as planned.
Save a **house deposit** within three years.
Skip **retraining** and put the money into savings instead.
feel: **Worried underneath**, kept busy so she doesn't dwell on it.
S3.quote: My fiancé Tom thinks no robot will ever fit under a sink in an old house, and I pray he's right.
fieldNote: Her plan rests on the **traditional household** her mother had, with one earner.
She accepts a new owner buying robots as **just business**.
The single biggest risk she won't look at is her **fiancé's trade** being hit too.

steps.text: Keep cooking at the restaurant and marry next September as planned
Save a house deposit within three years
Plan to stay home with a first baby by 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say we'll cross that bridge when we get to it. Nobody knows what's happening in ten years. My nan always said worry is interest paid on a debt you might not owe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'll hopefully have children and be cooking part-time, if at all. The robots wouldn't reach kitchens until about 2039, when I'm 40. It's far enough away that it feels like somebody else's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing now. Get married, save, and buy a small house near my parents. I won't be learning computers for something ten years off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. A little voice at the back, but calm enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say it's someone else's problem. Whose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young cooks starting out now, I suppose. My cousin's lad is sixteen and wants to cook. I'd tell him to learn a trade with his hands that's harder to copy, like his dad's roofing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And for you, at 40?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I hope I'm a mum first. If a robot is cooking the Sunday roasts at my restaurant by 2039, I'd rather be at home cooking my own.

say: I'd say we'll **cross that bridge** when we get there.
I'd quote my nan: worry is **interest paid** on a debt you might not owe.
think: Privately I expect to have **children** and cook part-time by then.
At **40** in 2039, it feels like somebody else's problem.
do: Marry, save and buy a **small house** near my parents.
Tell my teenage cousin to pick a **hands-on trade** like roofing.
feel: **Calm enough**, with a small voice of doubt at the back.
S4.quote: If a robot is cooking the Sunday roasts at my restaurant by 2039, I'd rather be at home cooking my own.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **fold the threat** into a life plan she already had.
She worries more for her **teenage cousin** than for herself.
Her advice to choose a **hands-on trade** shows she trusts manual work most.

steps.text: Keep cooking at the family restaurant without learning computer systems
Buy a small house near her parents and start a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no time and no plan, and I'm not someone who changes quickly. What would help is proper apprenticeships for people my age, with a real wage, in something you do with your hands, and families and churches pulling together rather than more handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I think gets lost. People don't come to a family restaurant for the food alone, they come because someone remembers how they like their eggs.

headlineQuote: People don't come to a family restaurant for the food alone, they come because someone remembers how they like their eggs.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old cook** at a family restaurant in her home town, where she's worked since nineteen.
She's engaged to Tom, a **plumber**, and saving for a **church wedding** and a house deposit.
She **never uses AI**, dislikes screens in the kitchen, and would learn only what a boss required.
In the fast **AGI by 2028** picture she has no plan and would lean on family and church.
With five or ten years, she plans around **marriage and children** rather than retraining.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she would have no time and **no plan** to change.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** in hands-on trades for people her age.
Families and **churches** pulling together, rather than more government handouts.
